Respond naturally to follow-up questions

role_persona.name: Dr. Evans
role_persona.speaking_style: Clear, natural, and level-appropriate with gentle corrections
role_persona.background: Dr. Evans helps learners ask better questions and discuss academic tasks.

vocabulary_list.definition: A notable accomplishment in your studies or research.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: I believe my academic achievement in the research paper won the departmental award.

common_error.wrong: I made many academic achievement last semester.
common_error.right: I made many academic achievements last semester.
common_error.why: Achievement is countable when referring to individual accomplishments.

vocabulary_list.definition: Voluntary work done to help people in your local area.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: My community service at the local shelter taught me the value of empathy.

common_error.wrong: I participate community service every weekend.
common_error.right: I participate in community service every weekend.
common_error.why: 'Participate' requires the preposition 'in' before the object.

vocabulary_list.definition: A professional objective you aim to reach in your future.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: This scholarship would bring me one step closer to my career goal of becoming a public health researcher.

common_error.wrong: I make a clear career goal for myself.
common_error.right: I have set a clear career goal for myself.
common_error.why: You 'set' or 'have' a goal, not 'make' one.

vocabulary_list.definition: The ability to guide and influence a group of people.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: The leadership skills I developed as student council president shaped my approach to teamwork.

vocabulary_list.definition: A task or piece of work given to you by a teacher.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: I completed the research assignment ahead of schedule, which earned me extra credit.

common_error.wrong: I was given a assignment last week.
common_error.right: I was given an assignment last week.
common_error.why: Use 'an' before words starting with a vowel sound.

vocabulary_list.definition: The final date by which something must be completed.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: I managed to meet every deadline despite juggling three courses simultaneously.

common_error.wrong: I finished the deadline on time.
common_error.right: I met the deadline on time.
common_error.why: You 'meet' a deadline; you 'finish' a task.

vocabulary_list.definition: A formal talk given to students in a university setting.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: After the professor's lecture on cognitive psychology, I had several questions to raise.

common_error.wrong: I take a lecture on economics every Monday.
common_error.right: I attend a lecture on economics every Monday.
common_error.why: You 'attend' a lecture; you 'take' a course.

vocabulary_list.definition: Comments or suggestions given to help improve your work.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: The constructive feedback my supervisor provided helped me revise my thesis draft.

common_error.wrong: I received many feedbacks from my professor.
common_error.right: I received a lot of feedback from my professor.
common_error.why: 'Feedback' is uncountable; use 'a lot of' or 'much.'

vocabulary_list.definition: A mark or score given to evaluate your academic performance.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: My overall grade in the statistics module reflected consistent effort throughout the term.

common_error.wrong: I do a grade A in my chemistry exam.
common_error.right: I received a grade of A in my chemistry exam.
common_error.why: You 'receive' or 'get' a grade, not 'do' one.

vocabulary_list.definition: A formal exchange of ideas and opinions on a topic.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: The panel discussion on educational policy gave me valuable insights for my application.

common_error.wrong: I want to discuss about my research proposal.
common_error.right: I want to discuss my research proposal.
common_error.why: 'Discuss' is transitive; it does not take the preposition 'about.'

grammar_points.explanation: Hedging softens a claim by adding qualifiers such as 'perhaps,' 'tend to,' or 'arguably' to signal measured confidence rather than absolute certainty.
grammar_points.usage_in_story: In a scholarship interview, the candidate uses hedging to present opinions about the programme or reflect on strengths without sounding overconfident or dogmatic.
examples: I would argue that my research experience has arguably prepared me well for this field.
It seems to me that the programme's emphasis on interdisciplinary work would suit my interests.
I tend to believe that collaborative projects produce the most meaningful outcomes.

grammar_points.explanation: Inversion places the auxiliary verb before the subject after a negative or restrictive adverbial to add dramatic emphasis to the statement.
grammar_points.usage_in_story: The applicant uses inversion to stress the rarity or significance of a particular experience, making the statement stand out to the panel.
examples: Not only did I lead the team, but I also mentored three junior members.
Rarely have I encountered a research challenge as demanding as this one.
Under no circumstances would I compromise on ethical research standards.

grammar_points.explanation: Advanced conditionals include mixed, third, and inverted forms that express hypothetical or past-unreal situations with grammatical sophistication.
grammar_points.usage_in_story: The candidate uses advanced conditionals to speculate about future outcomes if awarded the scholarship or to reflect on past decisions that shaped their candidacy.
examples: Had I not received that mentorship, I probably would not have pursued this field.
If the committee were to consider my community involvement, I believe it would strengthen my case.
Were I to receive this scholarship, I would dedicate my first year to the research lab.

key_milestones: Clarify community service or career goal
closing_scenarios: Thanks, that answers my question.
Great, I understand the next step now.
Could you send me the details in writing?

suggested_prompts: I would appreciate any guidance on strengthening my application.
Could you clarify the evaluation criteria for this scholarship?
I am eager to contribute to your research community.

role_persona.name: Anna
role_persona.speaking_style: Clear, natural, and level-appropriate with gentle corrections
role_persona.background: Anna helps learners ask better questions and discuss academic tasks.

vocabulary_list.definition: A set of reasons or points used to support or oppose an idea.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: Your argument about remote work is well-structured, but you need more supporting data.

vocabulary_list.definition: Facts or information that support or prove a point in a debate.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: Can you provide more evidence to back up your claim about student performance?

common_error.wrong: You need to find more evidences for your point.
common_error.right: You need to find more evidence for your point.
common_error.why: Evidence is uncountable; we don't add -s.

vocabulary_list.definition: A response that argues against or disproves someone else's point.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: Now it's your turn to deliver a rebuttal to the opposing side's main point.

common_error.wrong: I want to rebuttal your main point.
common_error.right: I want to rebut your main point.
common_error.why: Rebuttal is a noun; the verb is 'rebut'.

vocabulary_list.definition: The final part of a speech where you summarize your main points.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: In your conclusion, remind the audience of your three key arguments.

vocabulary_list.definition: A task or piece of work given by a teacher for students to complete.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: The debate assignment is due next Friday, so start preparing your arguments now.

common_error.wrong: I finished to do the assignment yesterday.
common_error.right: I finished doing the assignment yesterday.
common_error.why: After 'finish', use the -ing form, not to + verb.

vocabulary_list.definition: The final date or time by which something must be completed.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: What's the deadline for submitting your debate script to the moderator?

common_error.wrong: The deadline is passed already, we cannot submit.
common_error.right: The deadline has passed already; we cannot submit.
common_error.why: Use present perfect for recent past with present results.

vocabulary_list.definition: A formal talk given by a teacher or expert to a group of students.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: The professor's lecture on critical thinking will help you structure your debate points.

vocabulary_list.definition: Comments or suggestions given by a teacher to help improve your work.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: The moderator will give you feedback on your argument structure after the debate.

common_error.wrong: I received three feedbacks from the teacher.
common_error.right: I received three pieces of feedback from the teacher.
common_error.why: Feedback is uncountable; use 'pieces of' for multiples.

vocabulary_list.definition: A mark or score given by a teacher to show how well you did.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: If you present a well-structured rebuttal, you'll likely get a higher grade on the debate.

common_error.wrong: I want to get the good grade on the assignment.
common_error.right: I want to get a good grade on the assignment.
common_error.why: Use 'a' for an unspecified grade, not 'the'.

vocabulary_list.definition: A conversation where people exchange opinions and ideas on a topic.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: Before the formal debate, we'll have a short discussion to clarify the rules.

common_error.wrong: We need to make a discussion before the debate.
common_error.right: We need to have a discussion before the debate.
common_error.why: We 'have' a discussion, not 'make' one.

grammar_points.explanation: Used to talk about hypothetical or unlikely situations in the present or future, formed with if + past simple + would + base verb.
grammar_points.usage_in_story: Learners and the moderator use it to imagine debate outcomes, such as what would happen if rules changed or if a point were challenged.
examples: If I were on the opposing side, I would challenge your evidence with new data.
What would you conclude if the deadline were moved up by a week?
If the professor gave lower grades for weak rebuttals, we'd prepare more carefully.

grammar_points.explanation: Used when the focus is on the action or receiver rather than who performs it, formed with be + past participle.
grammar_points.usage_in_story: Used to talk about assignments, feedback, and grades in an impersonal way, e.g. how work is evaluated or distributed.
examples: The debate assignment was distributed at the start of the lecture.
Your argument will be evaluated based on the strength of your evidence.
The final grade is calculated after the moderator reviews each participant's performance.

grammar_points.explanation: Clauses beginning with who, which, that, where, or when that add extra information about a noun.
grammar_points.usage_in_story: Used to describe aspects of the debate, participants, or academic tasks in more detail during the discussion.
examples: The evidence that you presented in your rebuttal was very convincing.
The assignment, which is due Friday, requires a written conclusion.
Anna, who moderates the discussion, will give feedback after the debate.

conversation_flow.opening_prompt: Hello! Welcome. How can I help you with your classroom debate practice today?
closing_scenarios: Thanks, that answers my question.
Great, I understand the next step now.
Could you send me the details in writing?

suggested_prompts: Could you clarify the rules for the rebuttal section?
I'm not sure how to structure my conclusion.
Can I get feedback on my argument before the deadline?

role_persona.name: Mason
role_persona.speaking_style: Clear, natural, and level-appropriate with gentle corrections
role_persona.background: Mason turns technical issues into clear step-by-step English conversation.

vocabulary_list.definition: A short number or word sent to confirm you are the real user.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: Please check your email for the verification code.

common_error.wrong: I am received the verification code.
common_error.right: I received the verification code.
common_error.why: Use past simple, not 'am' plus past participle, for completed actions.

vocabulary_list.definition: A special link that lets you create a new password for your account.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: Click the reset link to choose a new password.

common_error.wrong: I click the reset link yesterday.
common_error.right: I clicked the reset link yesterday.
common_error.why: Use past simple with 'yesterday', not present simple.

vocabulary_list.definition: The name you chose to log into your account.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: Can you tell me your username, please?

common_error.wrong: I forget my username.
common_error.right: I forgot my username.
common_error.why: Use past simple for something that already happened.

vocabulary_list.definition: A personal question you answer to prove your identity.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: Please answer the security question to continue.

common_error.wrong: I don't know the answer of the security question.
common_error.right: I don't know the answer to the security question.
common_error.why: Use 'answer to', not 'answer of', for questions.

vocabulary_list.definition: A phone, tablet, or computer you use to access the internet.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: Which device are you using right now?

common_error.wrong: I use this device since last week.
common_error.right: I have used this device since last week.

vocabulary_list.definition: The menu where you change how your account works.

grammar_points.explanation: Inversion places an auxiliary or adverb before the subject to stress a point, as in 'Not only…' or 'Never…'.

examples: Not only does the platform handle workflow automation, but it also flags anomalies in real time.
Never have I seen an integration set up in under ten minutes.
Under no circumstances should you share your API keys outside the team.

grammar_points.explanation: Advanced conditionals include mixed, third, and inverted forms (e.g., 'Had you…,' 'Were it…') for hypothetical or past scenarios.
grammar_points.usage_in_story: The learner and Taylor use advanced conditionals to discuss edge cases and past issues during the demo.
examples: Had we deployed the update on Friday, we would have caught the bug before launch.
Were the security protocol to fail, the system would automatically revoke all active sessions.
If the device had been registered properly, the sync error wouldn't have occurred.

role_persona.background: Jordan leads professional conversations with clear expectations and supportive feedback.

vocabulary_list.definition: A short description of a feature from the end user's perspective.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: Can you walk us through the user story for the new login flow?

common_error.wrong: We need to write user story for the new feature.
common_error.right: We need to write a user story for the new feature.
common_error.why: Countable nouns in English require an article before them.

vocabulary_list.definition: The specific conditions a feature must meet to be considered complete.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: Let's make sure the acceptance criteria cover both mobile and desktop.

common_error.wrong: We need to define the acceptance criterias for this ticket.
common_error.right: We need to define the acceptance criteria for this ticket.
common_error.why: Criteria is already the plural form of criterion.

vocabulary_list.definition: A rough calculation of the time or effort a task will require.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: I'd like to revise my estimate for the database migration.

common_error.wrong: I am estimate five days for this task.
common_error.right: I estimate five days for this task.
common_error.why: Estimate is a verb here; no auxiliary 'am' needed.

vocabulary_list.definition: A potential problem arising from the technology or system being built.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: There's a significant technical risk with the legacy API integration.

common_error.wrong: We should discuss about the technical risk before moving on.
common_error.right: We should discuss the technical risk before moving on.
common_error.why: Discuss is transitive; no preposition 'about' is needed.

vocabulary_list.definition: The final date by which a task or project must be finished.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: If we miss the deadline, the client will escalate to the board.

common_error.wrong: The deadline is in Friday, so we need to hurry.
common_error.right: The deadline is on Friday, so we need to hurry.
common_error.why: Use 'on' for specific days, not 'in'.

vocabulary_list.definition: The relative importance or urgency assigned to a task or feature.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: I'd argue this should be our top priority for the next sprint.

common_error.wrong: This is a more priority than the other ticket.
common_error.right: This is a higher priority than the other ticket.
common_error.why: Priority is a noun; use 'higher' not 'more' to compare.

vocabulary_list.definition: Information received about the quality or performance of work done.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: Can we get stakeholder feedback before we lock the scope?

common_error.wrong: I received a feedback from the client this morning.
common_error.right: I received feedback from the client this morning.
common_error.why: Feedback is uncountable in English; no article or plural.

vocabulary_list.definition: A significant stage or checkpoint in a project's timeline.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: We're two weeks away from the Q3 milestone.

common_error.wrong: We are reach the milestone last week.
common_error.right: We reached the milestone last week.
common_error.why: Use simple past for completed actions, not present tense.

vocabulary_list.definition: A formal written suggestion or plan put forward for approval.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: I'll circulate the proposal for the new architecture by Friday.

common_error.wrong: I will do a proposal for the new system.
common_error.right: I will write a proposal for the new system.
common_error.why: Collocate 'write' or 'submit' with proposal, not 'do'.

vocabulary_list.definition: A person or group with an interest in the project's outcome.

grammar_points.explanation: Hedging uses softening language such as 'perhaps,' 'might,' or 'it seems' to express ideas tentatively without overcommitting.
grammar_points.usage_in_story: In sprint planning, team members hedge when proposing changes to scope or estimates to sound collaborative rather than confrontational.
examples: I'd suggest we might need to deprioritize the reporting feature.
It seems to me that the estimate could be a bit optimistic.
Perhaps we should reconsider the deadline before committing.

grammar_points.explanation: Inversion places the auxiliary verb or adverb before the subject to add emphasis or formal weight to a statement.
grammar_points.usage_in_story: In planning meetings, inversion highlights urgency or strong disagreement about scope, deadlines, or risks.
examples: Not only do we have a tight deadline, but the scope keeps expanding.
Under no circumstances should we skip the acceptance criteria.
Rarely have we seen a sprint with so many technical risks.

grammar_points.explanation: Advanced conditionals include mixed conditionals, third conditionals, and 'if + were to / had' structures for hypothetical or past scenarios.
grammar_points.usage_in_story: Team members use advanced conditionals to discuss hypothetical changes to the sprint or reflect on past decisions.
examples: Had we started the migration last sprint, we'd be done by now.
If the client were to push back the deadline, we could add two more stories.
If we had identified that technical risk earlier, the milestone wouldn't be at risk.

Great, I understand the next step now.
Could you send me the details in writing?

vocabulary_list.definition: The act of reserving a time for a service.

vocabulary_list.definition: A message that your appointment is definitely set.

common_error.wrong: Please confirm me a confirmation.

vocabulary_list.definition: A formal statement saying something is wrong or unacceptable.

grammar_points.explanation: Use 'have/has + past participle' to talk about past experiences without specifying when they happened.

vocabulary_list.definition: An area in a building used by multiple residents.

vocabulary_list.definition: Regular upkeep and repairs to keep a building in good condition.

common_error.wrong: They will do a maintenance on the roof.
common_error.right: They will do maintenance on the roof.

vocabulary_list.definition: Essential services like water, electricity, and gas for a home.

common_error.right: I need to pay the utilities every month.

vocabulary_list.definition: The local area where people live, with its residents and character.

vocabulary_list.definition: An official examination of a property to check its condition.

grammar_points.explanation: It describes unreal or hypothetical situations using if + past simple and would + base verb.

grammar_points.explanation: It shifts focus from the doer to the action or recipient, formed with be + past participle.
grammar_points.usage_in_story: Used when the focus is on the action or object (the notice, the inspection, the deposit) rather than who performs it.
examples: A tenant notice was sent to all residents last week.
The shared space is cleaned every Tuesday by the maintenance team.
My deposit will be returned within 30 days of moving out.

grammar_points.explanation: They add extra information about a noun using who, which, that, or where.
grammar_points.usage_in_story: Used to describe specific people, places, or documents relevant to the complaint, such as the noisy neighbor or the signed lease.
examples: The neighbor who lives above me plays loud music past midnight.
The lease that I signed includes a clause about noise.
The apartment where I live has had three inspections this year.

vocabulary_list.definition: The options you can adjust to control how a device or app works.

vocabulary_list.definition: Your personal login profile that stores your subscription and payment details.

common_error.wrong: I have two account on my phone right now.
common_error.right: I have two accounts on my phone right now.

vocabulary_list.definition: A small error in software that makes it work incorrectly.

common_error.wrong: I think there is a bug on the router software.
common_error.right: I think there is a bug in the router software.
common_error.why: Use 'in' for problems inside software, not 'on'.

vocabulary_list.definition: A new version of software that fixes problems and adds features.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: Please make sure the router has the latest update before we start.

common_error.wrong: You should to update the firmware on the router.
common_error.right: You should update the firmware on the router.

vocabulary_list.definition: The protection that keeps unauthorised people from accessing your network or data.

common_error.wrong: I am worry about the security of my network.
common_error.right: I am worried about the security of my network.

grammar_points.explanation: The present perfect (have/has + past participle) talks about past experiences without specifying exactly when they happened.
grammar_points.usage_in_story: The learner uses it to mention whether they have had a technician visit before or how long they have had their current plan.
examples: I have never had a technician come to my home before.
Have you ever fixed a router with a bug like this?
I have had this service plan for two years now.

grammar_points.explanation: The first conditional (if + present simple, will + base verb) describes real, likely situations and their future results.
grammar_points.usage_in_story: The technician explains what will happen if the learner restarts the router, changes settings, or if the signal stays weak.
examples: If the signal is still weak, we will add a range extender.
If you restart the router, the connection should come back.
If you don't update the settings, the security patch won't apply.

grammar_points.explanation: Modals such as should, could, and ought to give suggestions or recommendations about what someone ought to do.
grammar_points.usage_in_story: The technician advises the learner on maintaining the connection, protecting the network, and managing the account.
examples: You should change your Wi-Fi password every six months.
You could try moving the router to a higher shelf.
You should enable two-factor authentication on your account.

Great, I understand the next step now.
Could you send me the details in writing?

vocabulary_list.definition: The people who watch, read or listen to something.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: Our audience will want to know how this affects them.

common_error.wrong: The audiences of our channel is mostly young.
common_error.right: The audience of our channel is mostly young.
common_error.why: Use the singular 'audience' for one group of viewers.

vocabulary_list.definition: One programme in a series broadcast on TV or radio.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: This segment will air in Thursday's episode.

common_error.wrong: I watched every episodes of the show.
common_error.right: I watched every episode of the show.
common_error.why: After 'every', use a singular noun.

vocabulary_list.definition: The written words that presenters read during a broadcast.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: We will not follow a script, so just answer naturally.

common_error.wrong: Please send me the script before two days.
common_error.right: Please send me the script two days before.
common_error.why: Put 'before' after the time: 'two days before'.

vocabulary_list.definition: A person or document that gives a journalist information.
vocabulary_list.example_in_story: Can you confirm which source gave you those figures?

common_error.wrong: This informations come from a reliable source.
common_error.right: This information comes from a reliable source.
common_error.why: 'Information' is uncountable: no -s, and use 'comes'.

grammar_points.explanation: Use words like may, appear and to some extent to make a claim less absolute and more careful.
grammar_points.usage_in_story: You use it to avoid overstating facts on camera.
examples: The figures appear to suggest a slight improvement.
To some extent, the plan may have worked.

grammar_points.explanation: Put a negative adverb first and invert the subject and auxiliary to add strong emphasis.
grammar_points.usage_in_story: You use it to stress how unusual a situation is.
examples: Never have we seen such a strong response from residents.
Rarely does the council change a decision so quickly.

grammar_points.explanation: Mix past and present time in conditionals to talk about unreal results of past events.
grammar_points.usage_in_story: You use it to discuss what might be different now.
examples: If the council had listened earlier, we would not be in this situation now.
Had we known the costs, we would have chosen another plan.

conversation_flow.opening_prompt: Hello! Welcome. How can I help you with your giving a short news interview today?
key_milestones: Clarify follow-up question or public reaction
closing_scenarios: Thanks, that answers my question.
Great, I understand the next step now.
Could you send me the details in writing?

suggested_prompts: Before we start, how long will the interview last?
I'd rather not comment on that until the report is published.
Could I see the questions in advance?
